records.title: 9-2X 2.5L EJ253 Head Gasket External Leak (Subaru-Sourced)
records.description: The 9-2X Linear / 2.5i used the same 2.5L EJ253 SOHC engine as the contemporary Subaru Impreza/Forester/Outback. This engine has the well-known external head gasket leak — typically presents as oil seeping at the head-block joint, particularly at the front of the engine. Coolant leaks less common but possible. Symptoms appear 80,000-150,000 miles.
records.solution: Head gasket replacement (~$1,800-$2,800 at Subaru-experienced independent). Use Subaru OEM MLS gaskets (Mahle aftermarket also acceptable). ALWAYS resurface the heads — warped surfaces are common cause of recurrent leak. Timing belt, water pump, all idlers should be replaced at the same time since engine is apart.

records.title: 9-3 Direct Ignition Cassette (DIC) Failure
records.description: The Saab Direct Ignition Cassette — single integrated unit covering all four spark plugs — is a well-known wear item across 9-3 (and 9-5) from 1999 through end of production. Symptoms: misfire (often cylinder-specific then random), reduced power, check engine light. Failure rate climbs sharply after 80,000 miles. Saab DIC heat-shielding cracks; rubber boots fail.
records.solution: Replace DIC ($150-$350 OEM cassette, $80-$180 aftermarket — quality matters here, cheap units fail in months). DIY ~30 minutes with a 10mm hex socket. Always replace spark plugs at the same time (NGK PFR7S8EG or equivalent). Carry a spare DIC if traveling long distances — failure is sudden but the car limps home on the remaining cylinders.

records.title: 9-3 Second-Gen Front Lower Control Arm Bushing Failure
records.description: Second-gen 9-3 (Epsilon platform) front lower control arm rear (large) bushings wear and tear by 60,000-100,000 miles. Symptoms: clunking over bumps, steering wander, vibration through wheel, uneven tire wear. Saab supplies the bushing only as part of the entire control arm (not separately), so many independents replace the whole arm.
records.solution: Replace lower control arms as a pair (Lemförder OEM ~$120-$200 each, plus $200-$400 labor). DIY-friendly with a spring compressor and basic tools. Polyurethane aftermarket bushings (Powerflex) are more durable but transmit more NVH. Get a 4-wheel alignment after the job.

records.title: 9-3 Sentronic (Aisin AF33-5) 5-Speed Auto Failure
records.description: Second-gen 9-3 (2003-2011) Sentronic 5-speed automatic is the Aisin AF33-5. Develops harsh shifts, slipping, then total failure typically by 100,000-150,000 miles. Saab's "lifetime fill" claim was the prime contributor. Failure mode includes valve body wear and torque-converter shudder.
records.solution: Drain-and-fill ATF every 40,000-50,000 miles with Aisin AFW+ / JWS3309 (~$120-$200 DIY — ~6 quarts come out per service). If shifts are already harsh, valve body rebuild ($800-$1,500) or full transmission swap with used unit ($1,500-$2,800). New AF33 transmissions are hard to source for Saab post-bankruptcy — used is the practical option.

records.title: 9-3 Sunroof Drain Clog → Soaked Carpet → DICE/TWICE Module Failure
records.description: Second-gen 9-3 (2003-2011) sunroof drains clog with debris (pollen, leaves). Water then overflows into the headliner, runs down the A-pillars, soaks the carpet, and pools in the front footwell — directly under the DICE (Driver Information Central Electronics) and TWICE modules. Wet modules can short and cause a cascade of weird electrical faults (no-start, dead instrument cluster, ABS faults, etc.).
records.solution: Clear sunroof drains annually (compressed air from above, fishline gently from below). If carpet is wet, dry IMMEDIATELY — remove driver carpet and inspect the modules. Once a module is corroded the only fix is replacement and recoding ($300-$1,200). Aftermarket dehumidifier packs in footwell help in humid climates.

records.title: 9-3 B207 Turbo Bearing Failure
records.description: The Mitsubishi TD04 turbo on 2003-2011 9-3 B207 2.0L Turbo engines develops shaft-bearing wear around 100,000-150,000 miles, especially on Aero variants which run higher boost. Symptoms: high-pitched whine, oil consumption, blue smoke under boost. Often co-fails with the bypass valve diaphragm.
records.solution: Replacement turbo ($400-$800 reman, $800-$1,400 OEM new) plus oil-feed line ($50-$80) and gaskets. Total job ~$1,200-$2,000 at independent. Always replace the oil-feed line — old line is the most common reason a fresh turbo fails immediately. Bypass valve ($40-$80) at the same time.

records.title: 5-Speed Automatic Transmission Limp Mode / Valve Body Faults
records.description: The automatic 9-5 can drop into limp mode (locked in a single gear until restart) and develop slipping or harsh shifts. Early versions of the 5-speed automatic introduced around 2002 had valve-body and software issues; common triggers include the torque-converter lock-up solenoid, speed-sensor faults, and degraded fluid. In limp mode the car launches in a high gear with an unlocked converter and bangs into gear on upshifts.
records.solution: Diagnose for solenoid/speed-sensor codes; a revised valve body (2003+ units are far more durable) or solenoid replacement often resolves it. Critically, change to synthetic ATF every 50,000-60,000 miles to prevent recurrence.

records.title: 9-5 B235 Turbo Oil Sludge — Class Action Settlement
records.description: Early 2.3L B235 turbo Saab 9-5 (1999-2003 most affected) had an oil-sludge issue serious enough to trigger a class-action lawsuit and warranty extension. Root cause: undersized oil sump + tight PCV system + factory-recommended 10,000-mile oil change intervals combined to coke oil in the turbo oil-feed line. Many engines failed with seized turbos or spun bearings.
records.solution: Strict 3,000-5,000 mile oil intervals with full-synthetic 5W-30 (or 5W-40 for high-mileage) — Mobil 1 or Amsoil. Sludge-removal cycle (BG EPR, Liqui Moly Pro-Line) over multiple oil changes. Inspect the oil pickup screen if sump removed — heavy sludge means engine rebuild ($3,000-$5,000). Original class-action coverage long-expired.

records.title: Crankshaft Position Sensor (CPS) Hot No-Start
records.description: The crankshaft position sensor on the first-generation 9-5 (B235 engine) is a very common failure item. As it degrades it tends to fail when the engine is hot, producing the classic 'hot no-start': the engine cranks but will not fire when warm, then restarts after cooling. It can also cause intermittent stalling while driving, a real safety concern.
records.solution: Replace the crankshaft position sensor with an OEM/Bosch-quality part - cheap unbranded aftermarket sensors are reported to fail again within months. The sensor is relatively inexpensive but located awkwardly near the bell-housing.
symptoms: Hot no-start (cranks but won't start when warm)

records.title: 9-5 Direct Ignition Cassette (DIC) Failure
records.description: Same DIC failure mode as 9-3 — 1999-2009 9-5 with the B235 2.3L turbo (Linear/Arc/Vector NA variants are B205) suffers DIC degradation. Saab dealers used to stock these by the dozen. Often the first part to fail on a high-mileage 9-5.
records.solution: Replacement DIC ($150-$350 OEM, $80-$180 aftermarket). NGK PFR7S8EG plugs at the same time. Trionic 7 ECU on 1999+ models compensates for misfire well, so the car often limps home — but P03xx codes will accumulate. Some owners pre-emptively replace at 100,000 miles.

records.title: Direct Ignition Cassette (DIC) Failure
records.description: The Direct Ignition Cassette, which sits directly on top of the spark plugs and combines the coils into one unit, is a frequent failure point on the four-cylinder cars. Underhood heat and valve-cover gasket oil leaks contaminating the coil pack degrade the cassette over time, causing misfires, rough idle, hard starting and stalling. A failed cassette typically has a burnt smell and discoloration around the plug boots.
records.solution: Replace the Direct Ignition Cassette (use a quality OEM-grade unit) and renew the spark plugs at the same time, applying the correct Saab dielectric plug. Fixing any valve-cover gasket leak prevents repeat failures.

records.title: Engine Oil Sludge in 2.0T/2.3T Four-Cylinder
records.description: The B205/B235 four-cylinder turbo engines are notoriously prone to oil sludge buildup that clogs the fine oil-pickup screen in the sump, starving the engine of oil and leading to bearing or turbo failure. Contributing factors include an undersized/overworked PCV crankcase ventilation system, a catalytic converter mounted close to the oil pan that cooks the oil, and Saab's original long oil-change recommendation using conventional oil. Once the pickup screen is choked, oil pressure collapses and catastrophic engine damage follows.
records.solution: Install the updated PCV #6 breather kit, switch to full synthetic oil with short 3,000-5,000 mile change intervals, and if sludge is suspected drop the sump and clean it (including the oil-pickup screen) thoroughly. Severe cases require engine rebuild or replacement.

records.title: Fuel Line Leak from Damaged Pump Retaining Tabs - NHTSA Recall 07V087
records.description: NHTSA campaign 07V087 covers certain 2001-2005 Saab 9-5 vehicles whose fuel-pump retaining tabs for the fuel-line connections may have been damaged during production. A connection can loosen and leak fuel, creating a fire risk in the presence of an ignition source. Applicability and completion are VIN-specific; the combined campaign population must not be presented as a 9-5 owner-report count.
records.solution: If fuel is smelled or seen, switch off the engine, avoid sparks or flames, move people away and arrange safe towing or emergency assistance. Check the VIN at NHTSA or with an authorized service provider. For an open campaign 07V087, the recall remedy is installation of the specified retaining bracket at no charge; do not improvise a clamp or disturb a leaking connection. Do not buy a fuel pump, line, seal or bracket from this page; recall completion and the exact remedy must be confirmed by VIN.
symptoms: Fuel odor near the vehicle or cabin
Visible fuel at the pump or line connection
Open campaign 07V087 shown for the VIN
affectedSystems: Fuel-pump line retaining tabs and connections

records.title: SID Display Dead/Missing Pixels
records.description: The Saab Information Display (SID) and the automatic climate control display almost universally develop missing or fading pixels as the cars age, making the clock, trip computer, radio and ACC readouts hard or impossible to read. The root cause is the ribbon cable connecting the LCD to its circuit board: the silver conductive traces become brittle and flake off, breaking the connection to rows of pixels.
records.solution: Replace the LCD ribbon cable (cheap DIY kits exist, no soldering needed) or fit a replacement LCD module. Professional pixel-repair services are also available. The unit itself usually does not need full replacement.

records.title: 9-5 Saab Information Display (SID) Missing-Pixel Failure
records.description: 1999-2009 9-5 (and 1999-2003 9-3) SID — the small dot-matrix display in the center dash that shows radio info, climate, trip computer — develops missing pixel rows starting around 100,000 miles. The flex-cable connection between the LCD glass and PCB degrades. Often presents as horizontal "dropout" lines in the display.
records.solution: Rebuild option: send the SID to a specialist (BBA Reman, Module Master, or several European Saab specialists) for ribbon-cable resoldering — $80-$180 with return shipping. DIY repair kits with replacement flex-cable available for ~$30. Replacement used SID rarely fixes the issue — they age the same way.

records.title: Takata Driver Airbag Inflator Rupture - NHTSA Recall 16E005 / 16V063
records.description: Second-generation 2010-2011 9-5 models (and 2003-2011 9-3s) use Takata PSDI-5 driver-airbag inflators that can degrade over time. Long-term moisture exposure can cause the propellant to burn too aggressively, over-pressurizing and rupturing the metal inflator body during deployment. Ruptured inflators can spray metal fragments into the cabin, causing serious injury or death.
records.solution: Have the dealer replace the driver airbag inflator under the Takata recall, free of charge. Owners should check VIN status, as parts availability was delayed in early notifications.

records.title: V6 Ignition Discharge Module (IGBT) Overheating - NHTSA Recall 05V399/06V410
records.description: NHTSA campaigns 05V399 and 06V410 together cover specified 2001-2003 Saab 9-5 V6 vehicles with B308 gasoline engines. The campaign documents describe an ignition-discharge-module IGBT that can overheat and burn out, cause engine stall and increase crash risk; 06V410 expanded the V6 population. Applicability, campaign completion and the installed module version are VIN-specific and must not be inferred from symptoms alone.
records.solution: Check the VIN for open campaigns 05V399 and 06V410 and have the authorized recall inspection or module replacement completed if applicable. For a stall, no-start or ignition DTC on a vehicle with completed campaigns, diagnose module power, wiring, engine management and other causes using WIS before replacing parts. Do not buy an ignition discharge module from this page; VIN campaign status, B308 application, bank, installed module and diagnosis determine the remedy.
symptoms: Engine stall or no-start on an applicable B308 V6 vehicle
Open 05V399 or 06V410 campaign shown for the VIN

records.title: 9-7X Driver-Door Master Power Window Switch Fire Recall (NHTSA 12V-406 + 14V-404)
records.description: NHTSA recalls 12V-406 (2012 initial) and 14V-404 (2014 expansion) cover certain 2005-2007 Saab 9-7X (and shared GM siblings Chevy TrailBlazer, GMC Envoy, Buick Rainier, Isuzu Ascender — all GMT360 platform) for a driver-side master power-window switch where fluid entry can cause corrosion in the switch module, leading to a short, overheating, melted components, and fire. Multiple in-service fires reported, including some while the vehicle was parked.
records.solution: Check VIN at NHTSA recall lookup (12V-406 / 14V-404). Free dealer remedy: inspect part number on the door module and install a new switch module if affected. GM advised parking outside until the remedy is performed. If you smell burning plastic from the driver door, do not operate the window — get the recall fix scheduled immediately.

records.title: Classic 900 (1979-1993) Windshield Frame & Rear Wheel Arch Rust
records.description: Classic 900 (1979-1993) is notorious for rust at the windshield frame corners (especially below the trim moldings), the rear wheel arches, and the floor pan under the carpet. Once visible, rust is usually already advanced because the inner structure rots first. Salt-belt cars commonly have structural rust by 25+ years old.
records.solution: Annual inspection at the windshield frame (lift the trim moldings) and rear wheel arches. Treatment of pinhole rust early ($200-$500) is far cheaper than structural repair ($1,500-$5,000) once advanced. Convertibles have additional rust at the chassis stiffening members. SaabClub specialists in the US Northeast offer body restoration packages.
